figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 1. BldA-AdpA combination promoted the production of ascamycin in Streptomyces sp. 80H647. (A) Secondary structure of the tRNALeu
(UUA) molecule encoded by the bldA80H647 gene. The UUA anticodon is highlighted in orange. (B) The predicted structure of AdpA protein. The
AlphaFold2-predicted Streptomyces sp. 80H647 AdpA model (green) is aligned with the crystal structure of the Streptomyces griseus AdpA DNA-
binding domain in complex with its target DNA (white, PDB ID: 3W6V). (C) Metabolite profiling of the wild-type Streptomyces sp. 80H647 strain
and its derivatives introduced with the bldA and adpA genes. Abbreviation of gene origin: 80H647, Streptomyces sp. 80H647; Sc, Streptomyces
coelicolor A3(2); NUC, nuc gene cluster. The chromatograms were extracted from m/z 452 [M + H]+ for 1 and m/z 381 [M + H]+ for 2 using the
SIR mode in UPLC-MS analysis. (D) qRT-PCR analysis of the acmD, acmE, and acmF genes putatively responsible for aminoacylation reaction.
Streptomyces sp. 80H647 strains transformed with pKU492::rpsLp-adpA-bldA80H647 and pKU492 plasmids were cultured in PV8 medium for 1.8
days, and total RNAs were isolated. Error bars represent the standard deviation (sd) obtained from three independent replicates.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. Structure−function predictions for AcmD, AcmE, AcmF, and AlaRS2. (A) The overall architectures of the AlphaFold2-predicted protein
models. AcmD and AlaRS2 adopt the intact AlaRS-like architecture, whereas AcmF has a truncated AlaRS-like architecture. AcmE has an
aminopeptidase-like structure like the Xc-aminopeptidase shown in Figure S8A. The disordered N-terminal sequences of AcmF and AcmE were
omitted from the figure. (B) Close-up of the ATP binding amino acid residues in the aminoacylation domain. The AcmF residues represented by
green sticks are aligned with the residues of Aquifex aeolicus AlaRS (white sticks, PDB ID: 1YFR). The magnesium ions are represented by green
spheres. (C) Amino acid residues putatively responsible for alanyl-AMS binding in the aminoacylation domain. The residues of AcmF (green
sticks), AcmD (cyan sticks), and AlaRS2 (orange sticks) are aligned with the residues of E. coli AlaRS (white sticks, PDB ID: 3HXU).

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 3. AcmD-AcmF pair efficiently catalyze the aminoacylation of dealanylascamycin. (A) UPLC-MS analysis of the in vitro aminoacylation
reactions. The dealanylascamycin (2), L-alanine, ATP, and E. coli tRNA mixture were used as the substrates. The chromatograms were extracted
from m/z 452 [M + H]+ for 1 and m/z 381 [M + H]+ for 2 using the SIR mode. (B) Enzymatic reactions of AcmD-AcmF and AlaRS2-AcmF pairs
with different substrate 2 concentrations. The peak area at 263 nm was used to quantify the reaction product 1. Error bars represent standard
deviation (sd) obtained from three independent replicates. (C) AcmD and AcmF work separately but cooperatively to aminoacylate the
noncanonical substrate 2 without being inhibited.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 5. Mechanistic study of AcmF. (A) The proposed molecular mechanism of AcmF-catalyzed aminoacylation in ascamycin (1) biosynthesis.
Glu232 (COO−) forms a hydrogen bond with the alanyl moiety (α-NH3
+) of the Ala-tRNAAla substrate. An additional interaction of Gln219 (N)-
Ala (O) occurs. The aromatic rings of Trp100 and Phe104 stack with the 2-chloroadenine moiety of dealanylascamycin (2). The other residues are
involved in hydrophobic interactions. (B) Relative activity of AcmF mutants compared with that of the wild-type enzyme. The in vitro enzymatic
reactions were performed in the presence of AcmF or its mutants, AcmD, dealanylascamycin (2), L-alanine, ATP, and an E. coli tRNA mixture.
Error bars represent standard deviation (sd) obtained from three independent replicates.
